METHOD / Methods & Principles

How does terrain become
a comparable clue?

Data integrity screening: 175 of 295 legacy local SRTM candidates were excluded; 16,195 of 500,090 global ETOPO candidates were excluded (16,118 clipped at tile boundaries, 77 failed the existing land criterion after corrected sampling). The 60-arc-second ETOPO now uses pixel-center and periodic-longitude interpolation, and features were recomputed for 81,858 existing 80 km candidates; model weights are unchanged. Coordinate, display and export consistency passed numerical checks; this does not mean field positioning accuracy, original sensor coverage or surface material has been validated.

Pick a patch of lunar or Martian terrain and find candidates with similar shape in Earth elevation data. The figures, text and formulas below correspond to the actual search pipeline used by the current entry point.

RESEARCH UPDATE / 2026-10-11

New Mars image branch: tested, not yet connected to search

Trained on DoMars16k public landform labels; grouped by CTX image source and approximate source center, with 5,288 test images held out. Source centers are not precise crop footprints, so cross-geographic independence remains subject to this limitation.

Public labels and held-out set

No manual or expert scoring is added. All classification results apply only to this Mars image dataset; they do not represent Earth analogs, bare-rock lithology or mission suitability.

Measured results relative to the baseline

CNN + contrastive learning macro-F1: 0.420; texture-descriptor baseline: 0.374. Two classes have an F1 of zero; the confidence interval for the ablation that removes the contrastive loss crosses zero, so it cannot yet be confirmed that this loss yields a stable improvement.

Deployment threshold not yet met

Earth-domain validation, DEM/image/geology fusion, and unknown-class and missing-data tests are still lacking. Production search still uses the existing terrain and regional-condition pipeline.

Full English report, per-class results and experiment versions ↗

High confidence does not mean unknowns can be recognized: the rejection test was not passed

After calibrating the existing DoMars classification model on the validation set, test ECE fell from 0.1564 to 0.0303; however, the fixed threshold retains only 14.15% of test images, which still have 17.11% errors, and all 64 synthetic-noise images passed. This is a post hoc audit on an already-used test set, not a new held-out set; the model remains research-only, and its confidence values cannot be used to claim that unknown-class recognition has been validated.

English report, reliability diagrams, frozen thresholds and failure cases ↗
IMAGE + DEM / research experiment, not deployed

Teaching imagery and elevation to find the same patch of terrain

16,939 windows of about 200 m come from 15 existing sources. Imagery and DEMs are first aligned to a common grid, then split by geographic source group; this experiment validates same-location correspondence, not whether cross-planet sites are suitable for missions.

Formulas side by side: how is it trained and validated?

Per-window normalization

μ and σ are computed only from that window's valid cells; mask m preserves the locations of missing data. Image brightness has not been radiometrically calibrated across sensors.

train_paired_correspondence.py → preprocess()
x = m × clip((a − μ) / max(σ, 1), −5, 5)The input is stack(x, m).

Pulling together two observations of the same location

Batches of 64 same-source windows, τ = 0.1; positives are the image and DEM of the same window. Other windows act as instance (in-batch) negatives, which does not mean their landforms or mission relevance are dissimilar.

train_paired_correspondence.py → run() / cross_entropy
ℓᴵ→ᴰᵢ = −ln[exp(zᴵᵢ · zᴰᵢ / τ) / Σⱼ exp(zᴵᵢ · zᴰⱼ / τ)]
ℒ = (mean(ℓᴵ→ᴰ) + mean(ℓᴰ→ᴵ)) / 2

Rank at which the original window is retrieved

The paired window is searched for within the full same-source candidate pool; ties use the average rank. Results are averaged first within each source and direction, then equally weighted across the four test sources.

train_paired_correspondence.py → ranks()
MRR = mean(1 / rank)It is not accuracy, a probability of identical material, or a degree of NASA endorsement.
Same-location correspondence test: equal-weighted MRR over four sources; higher means the original paired window ranks nearer the top
MethodMRRPurpose
Correctly paired dual-branch0.278462This round's research model
Gradient descriptor0.089063Hand-crafted feature baseline
Mismatched-pair training0.020187Pairing-information control
Untrained network0.016591Initialization baseline

The MRR difference relative to the descriptor is 0.189399, with a four-source bootstrap 95% interval of [0.067376, 0.341397]. With missing imagery / missing DEM it drops to 0.011933 / 0.011988; this is a stress test, and there is not yet a calibratable missing-data rejection. The single-site Jezero observation is 0.248431 and cannot represent generalization across Mars.

No manual scoring is performed. All sources have previously been used by the project, so this cannot be called a fresh external test; full DEM/image/geology fusion and independent evidence of material and mission relevance are still lacking. Training and validation were both run on 192.168.31.145.

EARTH SURFACE EVIDENCE

Beyond desert ecoregions: published dune distribution

Added Gunn (2026) global dune-presence records on a native 0.1° grid, with 106,540 cells recording dunes. When 'Regions with recorded dunes' is selected, at least 60% of the 3×3 samples must fall in recorded cells, and results are then ranked jointly with terrain and the specified lithology.

This is a condition based on published data, not a new model automatically identifying sand. Dunes in part of a cell do not mean the whole cell is sand; unrecorded cells are not verified negatives either. The research data can serve only as regional-level positive/unlabeled data and cannot be directly converted into image pixel classification or cross-planet relevance ground truth.

01 / OVERVIEW

First, understand a single search

Imagery helps with orientation; elevation provides the shape-based ranking, and the specified region and lithology conditions also take part in retrieval.

01 Choose a patch of terrain

Pick a center on the Moon or Mars and set a square extent of 20, 40 or 80 km. Elevation is read at each grid point, in meters.

02 Compare shape and relief

Subtract the median height and scale by relief, preserving the shapes of ridges and basins; the raw height range is also fed into the model so differences in size are not ignored.

03 Search, then inspect side by side

Earth windows at the same scale are ranked by feature similarity; five spatially dispersed candidates are shown first, and more can be loaded. 3D terrain, red markers on Earth and the evidence table help check differences; save up to three candidates to compare side by side.

02 / SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE

System architecture: what is precomputed and what is computed on the fly?

03 / EQUATIONS

Formulas, meaning and code side by side

H is the 32 × 32 elevation matrix; P₉₀ and P₁₀ are the 90th and 10th percentiles. clip means restricting values to a specified range.

01 / Relief and elevation

Remove absolute elevation, keep terrain shape

Use the median height as the reference and divide by a robust height range. The R used by the model is at least 1 m to avoid division by zero on flat ground; the elevation relief shown on screen is the raw percentile difference.

lunar_pipeline.py → model_input()
R = max(P₉₀(H) − P₁₀(H), 1)
h = clip((H − median(H)) / R, −3, 3)
Example: P₉₀ = 900 m, P₁₀ = 100 m → R = 800 m. If the median height is 500 m and a cell is 700 m → h = 0.25.
02 / Second channel

Highlight where height changes quickly

Grid-point differences are computed from the normalized height so the model can read edges and changes in relief. This is a grid-gradient feature, not true slope expressed in degrees.

model_input() → np.gradient(height)
g = clip(√(gₓ² + gᵧ²) × N / 4, 0, 3)
X = stack(h, g)，N = 32
Model input shape: 2 × 32 × 32. The two channels are height and gradient.
03 / Feature encoding

Build a vector from shape and raw relief

The logarithm of relief is concatenated with the 24 features output by the convolutions. The fully connected layers output 24 dimensions, which are then normalized to unit length.

TinyTerrainEncoder.forward()
r = (ln(1 + R) − ln(501)) / 5
u = MLP([CNN(X), r])
z = u / max(‖u‖₂, ε)
R is substituted as its value in meters. MLP: 25 → 32 → 24; ε is a numerical safeguard for normalization.
04 / Similarity ranking

Compare the directions of two vectors

q is the query and e is an Earth candidate. The closer to 1, the more similar the vectors; this is not 'the probability that it is an analog site'. Candidates are compared only within the same kilometer scale.

web_server.py → scale_vectors @ vector
s(q, e) = (q · e) / (‖q‖₂ ‖e‖₂)
Unit vectors: s(q, e) = q · e
Region and lithology conditions and joint scoring are first applied across the full index; then up to 512 top-scoring candidates are taken, and duplicate nearby results whose centers are less than 1.5 × the window side length apart are excluded. Five spatial groups are shown first, and the complete grouped shortlist formed from up to 512 qualifying windows in this search can be loaded page by page.
Further reading: how is the model trained?

The same terrain is given 90° rotations, mirroring and a small amount of noise to form two views. Contrastive learning pulls together the vectors of views from the same window and separates them from other views in the batch.

ℒᵢ = −ln[ exp(zᵢ · zⱼ / τ) / ∑k ≠ i exp(zᵢ · zₖ / τ) ]

j is the paired view of i, τ = 0.16; the code is contrastive_loss() in train_tiny_lunar_encoder.py. This training objective is not equivalent to cross-body expert analog labels, nor does it guarantee full rotation invariance.

CONTEXT FUSION / fixed-weight joint ranking

Adding region and lithology to retrieval

Conditions are computed over the full same-scale index, not just used to filter the final five results. The conditions are analog targets set by the user and must not be interpreted as the system having identified sandy terrain on the Moon/Mars.

S = 0.65 × (cos(q, e) + 1) / 2 + 0.35 × mean(C)
C is the fraction of 3×3 regional samples that satisfy each enabled condition. Each condition must reach at least 60% (at least six of nine cells) to enter the ranking; with no conditions, ranking is by terrain only.

Deserts/xeric shrublands use the RESOLVE 2017 ecoregions map; lithology uses the GLiM 0.5° grid. If the lunar geologic map is dominated by Mare Unit (at least 60% of samples), a basic volcanic rock analog is suggested automatically; otherwise lithology is not guessed and users may specify it themselves. Geologic maps and lithology are not equivalent to exposed rock strata, dunes or mineral measurements.

The weights and thresholds are traceable design choices that have not yet been calibrated against cross-body expert annotations; this is a fixed-weight scoring layer, not a newly trained material-recognition neural network.

Why not search directly with photos?

Lighting, surface color and acquisition conditions may differ. This pipeline first compares shape using elevation; the imagery overlay only makes the location and surface easier for people to understand.

Is 32 × 32 the resolution?

It is the model input size, not the original measurement precision. Interpolating coarser elevation onto more grid points does not create detail out of nothing. The 64 × 64 display mesh is likewise limited by its source.

Does the search cover every location on Earth?

No. It queries a prebuilt index of Earth windows; coverage and sampling density depend on the scale and the data already prepared.

2D imagery side by side: synchronized viewing, without treating imagery as identification

Search results can expand Moon/Earth source imagery, with both sides zooming and panning in sync; switching candidates resets the view. For Mars, orthoimagery can be shown within the extent of the existing USGS CTX sources at Jezero and Olympus; it is projected in the Mars source coordinates, areas without imagery appear as a transparent checkerboard, and the valid-image-cell fraction, source pixel spacing, license and hash are displayed; where there is no coverage, missing data is still indicated. Acquisition dates and ground registration residuals have not yet been verified. Earth imagery is cropped and resampled to the actual extent returned by Esri, fixing an issue where the service altered the bounds to fit the output aspect ratio; this is not a validation of ground registration error. The Moon uses a blended display texture whose precise valid extent, source dates and native resolution have not yet been confirmed pixel by pixel, and it cannot be used for material classification.

02 / THREE WORLDS

Data resolution determines how fine the comparison can be

MOON

Moon

LOLA global elevation provides the large-area context; six LROC NAC stereo DTMs provide local high-resolution terrain. The global map shows the research anchors of the six sources; each source's local map shows the original DTM bounding extent and transparent no-data areas, offers a total of 178 prebuilt 3 km crop centers, and lets you click a 200/500/1000 m box within the local map; when prebuilt windows are insufficient, samples are taken on demand from the verified original DTM, and any box with missing cells is rejected. Adjacent crops may overlap and cannot be treated as full lunar coverage or independent samples.

LROC DTM footprints ↗
MARS

Mars

The USGS MOLA/HRSC blended DEM supports the Jezero/Gale large-area context; one CTX stereo DTM each for Jezero and Olympus Mons, at about 20 m native grid spacing, supports local 200 m–1 km research. The global map shows the anchors of the two CTX sources and one HiRISE source; the CTX local maps show the original DTM bounding extent and transparent no-data areas, and the HiRISE local map shows the stored 3 km crop; a total of 103 3 km crop centers can be selected, and you can also click a 200/500/1000 m box within the local map; when prebuilt windows are insufficient, samples are taken on demand from the verified original DTM, and any box with missing cells is rejected. The project's reconstructed Jezero version and the USGS version come from the same image pair and cannot serve as independent ground truth for each other.

USGS CTX DTM ↗
EARTH

Earth

ETOPO is used for global coarse screening; Copernicus GLO-30 is used for the legacy micro-topography search. USGS 3DEP 1 m bare-earth DEMs of Meteor Crater, Kilbourne Hole, Carrizozo, Amboy Crater, Big Pine, the Cima volcanic field, Death Valley Mars Hill, and Idaho's Craters of the Moon have been made into 2 m crops for the new 5 m/20 m/4 m high-resolution micro-topography search. Amboy and Death Valley Mars Hill are Mars analog sites with existing NASA research; Cima was included in NASA planetary geology remote-sensing research, but this site's small windows remain unvalidated; Carrizozo and Big Pine are research candidates.

USGS 3DEP 1 m ↗

The Cima region was included in NASA planetary geology remote-sensing research ↗；the JPL 1992 AVIRIS flight-line index ↗ also lists Cima. These sources are regional research leads; the actual overlap between the flight lines and this site's 3 km DEM has not yet been confirmed, and no spectra or point-by-point lithology labels have been obtained for that window.

The newly added Death Valley Mars Hill is a NASA-described dry alluvial Mars analog ↗, and serves on this site as a known reference site. Its 3 km USGS bare-earth DEM and geologic map/land cover only demonstrate that the data are comparable; they do not automatically label each small window as basalt or as a Mars-equivalent location.

Scale limits A 200 m box spans only about 7 cells in the legacy ~31 m grid; in the new version it spans about 40 cells at 5 m for Moon–Earth, about 10 cells at 20 m for CTX Mars–Earth, and 50 cells at 4 m for HiRISE Mars–Earth. USGS also cautions that the truly resolvable detail in CTX DTMs may be much coarser than the 20 m grid spacing; resampling cannot create details that were not originally there, such as boulders or pit openings.
03 / RETRIEVAL MODELS

Three geometric retrieval paths

Large-scale production prototype20 / 40 / 80 KM

TinyTerrainEncoder

6,424 parameters; compresses a DEM into a 24-dimensional vector and compares its cosine similarity with prebuilt Earth vectors. The model is trained on self-supervised data from lunar and terrestrial terrain; Mars queries are currently an exploratory transfer.

There are not yet any window-level expert positive/negative pairs across bodies, so the cosine score is not a "probability of identical geology".

2014 paper baseline200 M / 500 M / 1 KM

Geomorphon co-occurrence retrieval

10 local landform classes and a 55-dimensional co-occurrence signature, coarse-ranked by modified Wave-Hedges similarity, supplemented with the top 10 from each Earth site, then shape-checked with D4 rotations/reflections, with optional re-ranking by true metric relief and regional de-duplication. High-resolution mode searches Moon/Earth at 5 m, CTX Mars/Earth at 20 m, HiRISE Mars/Earth at 4 m, and 3DEP bare-earth data.

There are currently only eight Earth candidate areas of about 3 km; they use the same windows as the small model, but there is no cross-body expert blind test to judge which ranking is better.

Use the research version ↗

True relief mode: In addition to the original landform/small-model coarse-ranked candidates, Earth windows with similar P90–P10 relief are added; both sides are rebuilt at the same metric grid spacing, aligned over eight rotations/reflections, each has its median elevation subtracted, and they are ranked by unscaled elevation-difference RMSE. The original normalized-shape mode can still be selected; overlays can switch between a shared metric color scale or separate normalization, and list the metric relief and RMSE values. The metric error is only a DEM geometric difference, not geological or analog accuracy. The lunar research page also offers an optional conservative surface-evidence filter: windows that simultaneously meet ≥80% alluvium on the state map, ≥80% shrubland in NLCD, and ≤5% barren land are excluded from the top five displayed; Mars is not filtered by default, to avoid discarding potentially useful alluvial landforms. Among the 180 top-five pure-geometry results for the 36 lunar queries in the eight-area development set, 11 triggered this double conflict; after filtering, every query still has five results. This is a rule effect, not material or analog accuracy; the state map and land cover are coarse in scale, and passing the filter does not prove exposed rock.

Literature source

Jasiewicz, Netzel & Stepinski (2014), “Landscape similarity, retrieval, and machine mapping of physiographic units”, Geomorphology. This site adjusts the local line-of-sight radius for 200 m–1 km windows and does not reproduce the original paper's experiments bit-for-bit.

When calling something similar, specify in what respect

Landform geometry

Compares crater rims, slope, curvature, and relief at the same metric scale, and overlays DEMs to check spatial shape.

Geology and material

The eight Earth candidates now show the proportion of each USGS state geologic map unit intersecting the box, as well as the 30 m land-cover proportions from Annual NLCD 2024. The geologic map scale is far coarser than 200 m of ground rock, and class 31 mixes rock/sand/clay; neither is mineralogical ground truth.

Environment and mission

Aridity, ice and snow, shelter, accessibility, and the like must be evaluated according to the mission scenario; Earth environments can only simulate some operating conditions.

NASA POWER regional climate is shown for the eight Earth candidates; not yet included in the ranking

The next gate toward publication-grade results

A small-scale blind-evaluation package of 24 queries/120 pairs has been fixed, covering six lunar and two Martian locations at three scales each, using the two-site Earth candidate pool from before Carrizozo was added, with the 2014 baseline, the small model, and control candidates shown in shuffled order. Human scoring has been cancelled; moreover, the existing sites have already been used in the research, so no cross-body accuracy or novel-site discovery rate can be claimed. Two new geographic holdout sites have been frozen and vectorized, and await independent labeling and evaluation.

The eight-Earth-site version v6 has frozen 24 queries/120 pairs; the original two-site v5 is kept for version comparison. Both versions are cancelled historical human-scoring plans and cannot be treated as a validated geographic held-out set. Historical blind-rating plan cancelled v6 frozen protocol ↗ Historical blind-rating plan cancelled Enter the Cima surface blind review ↗To take part in the Cima blind review, please open the review page first, to avoid seeing the geologic-map answers below.

Annual NLCD 2024 is sourced from the USGS／MRLC 30 m land-cover product; at this stage, Esri's Collection 1.1 image service is used to preserve the original class pixels. This mirror runs through 2024 and differs from the 2025 Collection 1.2 that USGS has released. Search shows per-window pixel statistics; the optional dual-conflict screen combines the state map and land cover to exclude some candidates, but these data are not mixed into the geometric score. Geologic unit boundaries are provided by Macrostrat , retaining the USGS State Geologic Map Compilation original-map citation; 10 m area sampling does not increase the original map scale. The Idaho crop additionally incorporates the NPS 1:24,000 geologic GIS map, showing per window the polygon proportions of named lava flows such as Blue Dragon; the original map's nominal horizontal accuracy is about 12.2 m, and it is still not on-site ground truth for bare rock or minerals. For the same Idaho crop, we also obtained USGS four-band NAIP aerial imagery, using near-infrared and red bands to compute a per-window NDVI threshold fraction as an uncalibrated vegetation signal; the 2021 imagery and 2024 NLCD differ in date and definition, and NDVI is not a material classifier.

An offline window study of near-infrared NDVI from NAIP at the eight sites has been done, but after comparison with the coarser 2024 NLCD shrub class there is not yet enough basis to use the threshold as a vegetation or bare-rock screen; this extended index is not deployed and does not enter the ranking. View the eight-site NDVI audit ↗. Separately, the CMR footprint of the NASA HyTES L2 thermal-infrared emissivity product confirms that the 2014 Cima flight line overlaps about 69.6% of the area of this site's 3 km study area; in the current Moon–Earth 500 m candidate grid, 66 boxes fall entirely within that official footprint. This is only flight-line geometry and does not represent valid spectral pixels or lithology ground truth; the roughly 3.33 GB HDF5 source file has not yet been obtained, and a per-pixel material model cannot yet be trained or displayed. View footprint, candidate counts and sources ↗。

Cima also adds the USGS Indian Spring 1:24,000 geologic map ↗; unit proportions for each 200/500/1000 m candidate are built from the original Arc/Info polygons, showing mapped units such as basalt/hawaiite lava flows, pyroclastics and alluvium. The 1992 original map was digitized in 2002, and the original report does not specify the horizontal positional accuracy of geologic contacts; 10 m area sampling cannot improve the original map's accuracy, nor can it confirm present-day surface outcrops. This evidence is only for interpreting candidates and does not take part in the ranking. View source and index audit ↗。

05 / 3D RECONSTRUCTION

How to view the terrain in 3D

The current 3D view builds a mesh from real DEMs and drapes sourced lunar or Earth imagery onto the surface. Comparison mode uses the same horizontal and vertical meter scale on both sides and can switch between side-by-side, a co-located wireframe overlay, and per-cell relative height-difference coloring. The relative height difference is defined as Δh = (Earth elevation − Earth window median) − (Moon/Mars elevation − Moon/Mars window median), with colors clipped at the 90th percentile of |Δh|; it is a cross-site shape residual, not a measurement error at the same site. The 3D mesh is a sparse preview loaded on demand; the actual visual grid spacing is listed separately on the page and should not be misread as the full resolution of the original DEM. High-resolution results can open a standalone 3D mission scenario, where you click on the actual DEM mesh to place a NASA Apollo Lunar Module, the Perseverance rover or an HDU display model, and switch to the same vertical exaggeration. Each result can be downloaded as a Markdown site card that records the selection center, ranking, land-cover and climate sources, and limitations. The models only convey scale and layout concepts; there is no certification of bearing capacity, hazardous boulders, illumination or landing safety. Skyfall-GS multi-view 3D Gaussian Splatting and diffusion refinement have not yet been completed on this site; the textures in the 3D display do not take part in the current search ranking.

For the eight Earth study areas, the microterrain 3D page drapes the RGB of USGS four-band NAIP aerial imagery, sampled at 2 m, onto the 3DEP DEM, aligned to the retrieved D4 orientation; source image years are 2021, 2022 or 2023 depending on the site and cannot be treated as contemporaneous surface observations. Sources and hashes for the eight sites ↗. Jezero and Olympus both drape the ~20 m grayscale orthoimage from the same USGS CTX DTM product back onto the Mars DEM. The six lunar NAC DTMs each also have a grayscale orthoimage from the same product, with native grid spacing of about 2–5 m; the Thiel image has one fewer row at its southernmost edge than the DTM, so coverage is checked box by box on request. These are georeferenced displays of published imagery: brightness includes illumination and shadow, and is not natural-color Martian material, per-pixel lithology, or Skyfall-GS multi-view synthesis. The research-pilot 3DGS for Mars Jezero has a PSNR of 11.76 dB on 54 held-out images and has not yet passed the geometric and appearance validation needed to substitute for the DEM.

Original methods, negative results and data limitations are retained; each of the numbers below corresponds to a different research version.

03B / NEW TINY MODEL

Small-scale encoder with 30,024 parameters

Self-designed / locally trained32-D VECTOR

TinyMorphEncoder

Same-scale DEM, median-normalized elevation, slope and curvature are converted into a 32×32×3 input, and four small convolutional layers output a 32-dimensional unit vector. Earth candidates are vectorized offline in advance; at query time, cosine similarity coarse-ranks the top 40 of the whole pool + the top 10 per site, followed by D4 fine ranking on true height difference or normalized shape, and regional de-duplication.

The model is trained self-supervised only on same-window rotations/noise and co-located 5 m/20 m pairs from Meteor Crater; there are no cross-body positive/negative labels.

Whole-site held-out225 PAIRS

What has been measured so far

Schrödinger, Olympus Mons and Kilbourne Hole are entirely held out of training. On 225 held-out windows, after rotation and Earth cross-resolution transforms, same-window retrieval Recall@1 is 96.0% and Recall@5 is 100%.

This measures only consistency under input transforms; it is not Moon/Mars–Earth analog accuracy, geologic-origin agreement rate, or real-site discovery rate.

03D / MATERIAL MODEL GATE

First counter-evidence for the material model

Earth field samples × airborne spectra163 PARAMETERS

Co-registering XRD and AVIRIS

Uses 16 pre-specified bands of NASA AVIRIS-Classic 2011 surface reflectance, paired with XRD mineral abundances from USGS San Juan hand samples; held out as whole groups by three field locations. The network has only 163 parameters and is compared under the same protocol against a linear model and a spectral absorption-depth baseline.

The samples and the airborne observations are several years apart, and pixels are mixed surfaces; samples at the same coordinates may also have different XRD labels.

First frozen evaluationNot deployed

Loading material research records…

Loading first-round results for independent field locations.

This experiment measures hand-sample mineral targets only along a single San Juan flight line on Earth and cannot be interpreted as a Moon/Mars–Earth material similarity rate; the results did not pass the deployment gate, so they do not enter the search ranking or the material panel.

Data and frozen protocol

Source data: NASA AVIRIS-Classic L2 ↗、USGS Data Series 595 field XRD ↗. We publish this run's pre-frozen protocol ↗、the complete first evaluation ↗ and the weights audit file ↗; the model weights are not used by this website to determine the material of Cima or of any Moon/Mars window.

SURFICIAL MAP / AMBOY

Distinguishing lava bedrock from surface cover

Amboy adds the USGS 2006 surficial geology GIS ↗. The original map is 1:100,000 and includes composite units, for example aeolian sand or slope deposits over volcanic rock; therefore "basaltic rock below" cannot be read directly as meaning the box surface is exposed basalt. In the current 3 km crop, about 80.4% of the area is the mapped unit "young aeolian sand and slope deposits over basaltic volcanic rock"; 100 of the 121 500 m candidates are dominated by this unit. This site computes the mapped-unit proportions for each 200/500/1000 m candidate from the original polygons, and they are not added to the geometric ranking. The accompanying field observation data have no points within the current 3 km crop; the mineralogy and outcrop status of the small windows remain unknown. View sources, units and hashes ↗

04D / EXTERNAL GEOGRAPHY

New geographic holdout: fix first, then compare

Before looking at any model ranking, Earth coordinates were fixed for two sites from NASA analog contexts: the Lava Beds volcanic area and the Pilot Valley salt flat. USGS 1 m bare-earth elevation for each was cropped to 3 km/2 m and converted into 200/500/1000 m candidates at Moon–Earth 5 m and Mars–Earth 20 m; the 2014 landform signatures and the trained TinyMorphEncoder weights remain unchanged. Both sites exist only in a separate research folder and have not yet been added to the public search library, model training or tuning. The fixed coordinates for Kīlauea have no valid pixels in the selected 2017 3DEP layer; the failure record is retained and a USGS 2019 lidar source is being investigated separately.

This is a geographic and environmental held-out set, not an independent-sensor held-out set, and there are no expert per-window positive/negative labels of any kind. Neither Pilot Valley's saline environment nor the subsurface caves of Lava Beds can be directly demonstrated from surface elevation vectors. Human blind rating has been cancelled; without independent relevance labels, a cross-body analog accuracy still cannot be reported. 04E / FINE MARS TERRAIN

HiRISE Jezero: pushing the Mars 200 m comparison to a 4 m grid

From the official HiRISE Jezero stereo DTM product ↗, a ~3 km crop center (18.3°N, 77.53°E) was fixed in advance, and the ~1.01 m original elevations were saved using HTTP range reads; the original crop has 100% valid pixels. After projection onto a 4 m comparison grid referenced to the selected area's center, about 98.4% of the whole grid is valid; each 200/500/1000 m box additionally requires all pixels to be valid, so edge boxes with missing cells are not searchable. The grayscale HiRISE orthoimage from the same product is saved as a ~2 m crop and draped back onto the 3D DEM; the pixel origins of the original image and the DTM differ by about 1.5 m. Image brightness is not a mineral or lithology label.

Indexed on the same 4 m grid together with eight USGS 3DEP 1 m bare-earth datasets: 200 m is 50×50 cells with 6,728 overlapping candidates; 500 m is 125×125 cells with 968; 1 km is 250×250 cells with 200. Each window has 55-dimensional geomorphon co-occurrence features and a 32-dimensional vector from the same frozen 30,024-parameter TinyMorphEncoder. Users can switch between the two coarse rankings, then fine-rank with D4 rotation/reflection on true height difference in meters or on relative shape. Geologic map, NLCD and NAIP NDVI evidence has been resampled to the exact center and box of each 4 m Earth candidate and is kept separate from the geometric ranking; the original map-sheet scale, 30 m class pixels and differing image years still limit material interpretation. The Earth 3D NAIP textures are also taken from the same candidate center.

Co-located evidence audit: the old nearest-20 m-window mapping had a 95th-percentile center distance of about 97.65 m at the 500 m scale; after switching to exact candidate centers, 14 primary geologic map units and 5 optional conflict-filter results change among 968 overlapping windows. Overlapping windows are not independent samples; these differences only show the importance of evidence registration, and are not an analog hit rate or material classification accuracy.

This is still an exploratory retrieval over eight Earth development areas, not a global search, a rock-material prediction, or a confirmed Moon/Mars–Earth analog. A 1 m elevation grid spacing does not mean 1 m rocks can be identified; HiRISE and 3DEP also have different measurement conditions. The v7 human blind review has been cancelled; the existing data cannot support a cross-body hit rate.

04F / BLIND RETRIEVAL REVIEW

HiRISE 4 m: cancelled blind-review plan

Eight Jezero query centers were fixed before viewing the held-out rankings, and each center compares 200/500/1000 m windows. 3DEP elevation for two new Earth regions, Lava Beds and Pilot Valley, was rebuilt into a 4 m candidate library: the three scales have 1,680, 241 and 49 overlapping windows respectively. Reusing the frozen 2014 landform features and the 30,024-parameter TinyMorphEncoder, each of the two methods selects two items, plus one sampled control; each question has five items in shuffled order. The public packet has 24 questions and 120 pairs; methods and candidate locations appear only in the non-public answer key.

This section is a historical protocol. Human rating was cancelled under plan 12.11; no ratings are being recruited or collected, and there are no rating results to analyze. Acceptance instead relies on traceable public labels, model comparisons and automated operational tests; the existing data still do not support a cross-body analog accuracy. Mars uses only one site, Jezero, which was involved in development; there are also only two Earth held-out areas, so the results cannot be extrapolated to global terrain or prove rock material, caves or base safety.
